judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's version of House Bill 121, a Texas school safety bill. This was the House's last vote on it. The House agreed 97-38, the governor signed it, and it took effect September 1, 2025. Texas already required an armed peace officer at each school campus during school hours. A district that cannot meet that rule may claim a good cause exception and use another plan. This law makes that exception expire after one year, so the school board must review and renew it. An alternative plan may use a school marshal or a trained, armed district employee or contractor. New security staff get 90 days to finish the required training, instead of 180. Texas Education Agency inspectors became peace officers, but only for safety monitoring and emergency coordination. A threat assessment team reviewing a special education student must include someone who knows that student's disability. A threat assessment is a review of whether a student may be dangerous. Teams must report a serious risk of violence to the superintendent right away. Districts may spend state school safety money on security staff, building upgrades, and suicide prevention. The Senate had dropped the House's new child abuse reporting rules for school employees.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 1586 in the Texas House. The law makes the state health department post the school vaccine exemption form online for anyone to print. People can still request a blank form in writing, and cannot be asked for any information. It drops the copy-proof seal on the form and bars the state from keeping requesters' names. It did not change who qualifies for an exemption. The House passed it 83-54, the Senate agreed, and the law took effect September 1, 2025.

People can still request a blank form in writing, and cannot be asked for any information. It drops the copy-proof seal on the form and bars the state from keeping requesters' names. It did not change who qualifies for an exemption. The House passed it 83-54, the Senate agreed, and the law took effect September 1, 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 5033. It ends state agencies' duty to run car emissions inspections only if Congress removes the federal requirement or a constitutional change lets states block such programs. Until one of those events happens, current inspection rules stay in force. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 101-45.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1036, which makes home solar sellers register, carry insurance, and list the licensed installer and last day to cancel in each contract. Buyers get five business days to cancel free, and sellers cannot lie or pretend to represent a utility or government office. The state may order refunds and fines up to $2,500, or $10,000 when the buyer is 65 or older. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 94-37.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 14, which created a governor's office to help agencies cut needless rules. Agencies must write proposed rules plainly and list them in a searchable public database, and a court may cancel a rule if the agency skipped required steps. Courts must decide what laws and agency rules mean without favoring the agency's view. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 97-51.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on the final version of Senate Bill 2024, a law on vapes marketed to children. The Texas House adopted the compromise 96-35. The law raised this crime from a Class B to a Class A misdemeanor. It bars selling or advertising a vape whose package shows cartoon characters, a celebrity name or image, or pictures of candy or other food. It also bars vapes shaped like school supplies, phones, watches, headphones, clothing, backpacks, cosmetics, or toys. It bars vapes made in, or advertised as made in, China or another country the United States names a foreign adversary. It bars vapes mixed with cannabinoids, alcohol, kratom, kava, mushrooms, or tianeptine. The governor signed it and it took effect September 1, 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 2835. It lets cities approve an apartment building with one stairway when it has no more than six stories above grade and four homes per floor. It must have stairway sprinklers meeting National Fire Protection Association Standard 13, two-hour fire-rated stairway enclosures, one-hour fire-rated hallways, an escape opening on each floor served by the single exit, and smoke and fire alarms, despite local code changes. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 81-57.
